lead: Sheet metal and plastics shaping turn flat sheets or polymer pellets into useful parts. After this unit you can read a forming operation, choose the main process variables, and estimate force, blank size or cycle output for simple cases.
about: The unit moves from how much a sheet can deform to the operations that cut and shape it, then to plastics. Chapter 3.1 defines formability with flow stress and forming limits. Chapter 3.2 uses shearing to cut blanks and holes, and fixes the blank that later operations use. Chapter 3.3 bends that blank, with bend allowance and springback. Chapter 3.4 deep draws a cup and checks draw ratio, blank holder force and ironing. Chapter 3.5 adds stretch forming, embossing and coining for skin panels and fine surface detail. Chapter 3.6 changes material to thermoplastics: injection moulding makes discrete parts in a cycle, extrusion makes continuous profiles.

chapters.idea: Formability is the safe amount of strain a sheet can take before local necking or tearing; it is judged by strain hardening, normal anisotropy and forming limit diagrams.
chapters.depth: Sheet metal operations start with a blank, a punch and a die; define blank, punch, die and clearance. Cover the power law σ = Kεⁿ, where σ is true stress in MPa, K is strength coefficient in MPa, ε is true strain and n is strain-hardening exponent. Define normal anisotropy r = ε_width/ε_thickness (Lankford coefficient), where ε_width and ε_thickness are true strains in width and thickness; high r resists thinning. Cover the forming limit diagram (FLD) with major strain ε₁ and minor strain ε₂; the forming limit curve separates safe and failed strain paths. Mention the tensile test and Erichsen cupping test as formability tests. Some syllabi call this sheet metal operations overview.

figure.aria: Plot of flow stress rising with true strain, following the power law with K equal to 500 megapascals and n equal to 0.20.

chapters.example: A steel sheet follows σ = 500ε^0.20, with σ in MPa. Find the true stress at ε = 0.20 and state what happens at that strain if necking begins when ε = n. Answer: σ = 500 × 0.20^0.20 = 362 MPa; necking starts at ε = n = 0.20.
chapters.trap: Using engineering strain or tensile elongation as the only formability measure; the FLD needs major and minor true strains, and n is not the same as r.
chapters.prereq: Unit 2: plastic deformation and true stress–true strain.
chapters.leave: Detailed yield criteria and rolling to Unit 2; blanking force calculation to 3.2.

chapters.idea: Punching and blanking are shearing operations that cut a closed contour; the same tool makes a hole in punching and a part in blanking, and clearance controls the cut edge.
chapters.depth: Define shearing, blank, punch, die and clearance. Punching (piercing) removes a hole; the punched slug is scrap. Blanking cuts the required blank; the blank is product and the strip is scrap. Cover notching, trimming, slitting and shaving as related shearing operations. Clearance is a small fraction of thickness, often about 5% to 10% per side depending on material; too little clearance gives secondary shear and burr, too much gives heavy burr and rollover. Force F = τ × L × t, where F is in N, τ is ultimate shear strength in N/mm², L is cut perimeter in mm and t is thickness in mm. A shear angle on the punch reduces peak force. Describe cut-edge zones: rollover, burnish, fracture and burr.

figure.aria: Tree separating shearing into punching, where the hole is scrap, and blanking, where the cut blank is the product.

chapters.example: A 2.0 mm thick steel sheet is punched with a 50 mm diameter hole. The ultimate shear strength is 300 N/mm². Find the punching force. Answer: L = π × 50 = 157.1 mm; F = 300 × 157.1 × 2.0 = 94,248 N ≈ 94.2 kN.
chapters.trap: Using tensile strength instead of shear strength, or using the hole area rather than perimeter times thickness.
chapters.prereq: 3.1 for sheet strain limits; Unit 2 for shear strength.
chapters.leave: Press construction and press tonnage selection to Unit 5; die design details to tool design.

chapters.idea: Bending forms a sheet along a straight line; the blank must include bend allowance, and springback must be compensated by overbending.
chapters.depth: Define bend line, bend radius R (inside radius in mm), bend angle θ in degrees, neutral axis and K-factor (position of neutral axis, typically 0.33 to 0.5 of thickness). Bend allowance BA = (π/180) θ (R + Kt), where BA is in mm and t is sheet thickness in mm. Bend deduction relates outside dimensions to flat length. Springback is elastic recovery; it increases with high yield strength and small thickness; compensation uses overbend or bottoming. Minimum bend radius depends on ductility and thickness; edge cracking occurs if the bend line is too near the edge. Methods: V-bending, edge bending and roll bending. Some syllabi call this bending of sheets.

figure.aria: Block diagram of V-bending: punch presses the sheet into a V-die, and the bent part keeps a small elastic springback.

chapters.example: A 2.0 mm thick sheet is bent to 90° with inside radius 4.0 mm. Take K = 0.40. Find the bend allowance. Answer: BA = (π/180) × 90 × (4.0 + 0.40 × 2.0) = 1.5708 × 4.8 = 7.54 mm.
chapters.trap: Using outside radius or forgetting K; also treating springback as a bend allowance error.
chapters.prereq: 3.1 for ductility and 3.2 for blank edges.
chapters.leave: Press brake operation to Unit 5; deep drawing curvature to 3.4.

chapters.idea: Deep drawing pulls a blank into a die to make a cup; draw ratio, blank holder force and ironing decide whether the cup wrinkles, tears or thins.
chapters.depth: Define deep drawing, cup drawing, blank diameter D_b, punch diameter D_p, draw ratio DR = D_b/D_p and reduction = 1 − D_p/D_b. Estimate blank diameter by equating cup and blank surface area: D_b = √(d² + 4dh) for a thin cylindrical cup with diameter d and height h (ignore corner radius); all lengths in mm. Blank holder force prevents wrinkling; too much causes tearing. Redrawing uses smaller punches; ironing thins and smooths the wall by forcing the cup through a slightly smaller die. Defects: wrinkling, earing, tearing and orange peel. Hydroforming uses fluid pressure instead of a punch; some syllabi list it here.

figure.aria: Block diagram of cup drawing: a blank is clamped by a blank holder, a punch pushes it into a die, and a cup is formed.

chapters.example: A cylindrical cup of diameter 50 mm and height 60 mm is to be drawn from a 2.0 mm sheet. Estimate the blank diameter using D_b = √(d² + 4dh). Find the draw ratio for the first draw. Answer: D_b = √(50² + 4 × 50 × 60) = √14500 = 120.4 mm; DR = 120.4/50 = 2.41, so a first draw may need redrawing.
chapters.trap: Using punch diameter as blank diameter in draw ratio; forgetting blank holder force; ignoring that ironing changes wall thickness.
chapters.prereq: 3.1 formability, 3.2 blank, 3.3 bend radius at cup corner.
chapters.leave: Hydroforming details to advanced study; press selection to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: Stretch forming pulls a clamped sheet over a form block, while embossing and coining press sheet between closed dies to copy surface detail; coining also changes thickness.
chapters.depth: Stretch forming: sheet gripped at edges and pulled over a form block; tensile stress stretches the sheet to the block shape; springback is lower than in bending; used for aircraft skins and large auto panels. Define engineering strain e = (L_f − L_0)/L_0 and true strain ε = ln(L_f/L_0), where L_f is final length and L_0 is original length. Embossing: shallow raised or sunken pattern from matched dies; mostly surface flow with little thickness change; used for labels and panels. Coining: high pressure closed-die forming with controlled metal flow in all directions; thickness changes; used for coins, medals and precision parts. Some syllabi add hydroforming as fluid-pressure forming; it belongs with sheet tensile forming.

figure.aria: Block diagram of stretch forming: grips pull a clamped sheet over a form block, giving a stretched skin part.

chapters.example: A 1.2 mm thick sheet is stretch formed from 800 mm to 860 mm between grips. Find engineering strain and true strain. Answer: e = (860 − 800)/800 = 0.075 = 7.5%; ε = ln(860/800) = 0.0723.
chapters.trap: Saying embossing and coining both keep thickness constant; coining intentionally changes thickness. Also using engineering strain as true strain in large stretch.
chapters.leave: Hydroforming and high-energy forming to advanced study; die materials to tool design.

chapters.idea: Thermoplastics are shaped by melting polymer and forcing it into a closed mould in cycles (injection moulding) or through a die continuously (extrusion).
chapters.depth: Define polymer, thermoplastic, thermoset, melt and viscosity. Injection moulding: hopper, barrel, reciprocating screw, heaters, nozzle, mould and clamp; cycle: fill, pack, cool, eject; cooling dominates cycle time. Defects: short shot, flash, sink marks, weld lines and warpage. Extrusion: screw extruder, die, melt pump, cooling and haul-off; continuous products: pipes, films and profiles. Some syllabi add compression moulding for thermosets: charge placed in a heated mould, pressure applied, cure; it is cyclic, not extrusion. Do not cover mould design in depth.

figure.aria: Block diagram of injection moulding: pellets feed a heated screw barrel, melt passes through a nozzle into a mould, and a part is ejected.

chapters.example: An injection moulding cycle has fill 2 s, pack 3 s, cool 15 s and eject 5 s for one cavity. Find cycle time and output per hour. Answer: cycle = 2 + 3 + 15 + 5 = 25 s; output = 3600/25 = 144 parts/hour.
chapters.trap: Confusing injection moulding (cyclic, discrete parts) with extrusion (continuous profile); ignoring cooling time.
chapters.leave: Polymer chemistry and mould design to polymer courses; compression moulding details to advanced study.
